Transparent photovoltaic (TPV) devices represent a promising advance in
photovoltaic technologies, particularly in building-integrated photovoltaics
(BIPV). Unlike conventional photovoltaics, which primarily prioritize efﬁciency,
TPV must balance between efﬁciency, transparency, and aesthetics. These
additional dimensions introduce unique challenges on device architecture.
This article reports the development of wide-bandgap, inorganic-based TPV
devices integrating ultrathin hydrogenated amorphous silicon (a-Si:H) as a
transparent absorber, with carrier selective contacts and transparent elec-
trodes. The article analyzes how absorber thickness inﬂuences the electrical,
optical, and aesthetic performance of devices, evaluating key parameters in
TPV such as light utilization efﬁciency (LUE), average photopic transmittance
(APT), color rendering index (CRI), and electrical properties such as power
conversion efﬁciency (PCE). The device structure is SLG/FTO/AZO/a-SiCx(n)/
a-Si:H/V2Ox/AZO. This approach results in PCE ranging from 1.7% with an
APT of 60% to a PCE of 4.1% with an APT of 28%, yielding LUE values between
0.9% and 1.3%. Device characterization encompasses optical spectropho-
tometry, J–V measurements under standard test conditions, spectral response
analysis, and variable illumination measurements (VIM). Additionally, color
characterization is conducted using CIE 1931 color space maps to determine
the chromaticity coordinates, CRI, and the variation of color as a function of
absorber thickness.

The devices studied in this research are based on the integra-
tion of a nanometric hydrogenated amorphous silicon layer
(a-Si:H)[9] that is sandwiched between two charge-carrier selec-
tive contacts: a hole transport layer (HTL) and an electron trans-
port layer (ETL).[10] These selective layers play a crucial role in
separating the photogenerated charge carriers. The HTL allows
the ﬂow of holes while blocking electrons and the ETL does a
complementary work, allowing the pass of electrons while
blocking holes. Various materials have been investigated for these
layers, including MoOx,[11] V2Ox,[12] and NiOx
[13] as HTLs, and
silicon-doped, AZO and TiOx as ETLs. From this study, the opti-
mal device conﬁguration includes vanadium oxide (V2Ox) as the
HTL[14] and n-type phosphorous-doped hydrogenated amorphous
silicon carbide (a-SiCx(n)) as the ETL.[15] The transparent conduc-
tive oxides (TCOs) chosen to complete the device were ﬂuorine-
doped tin oxide (FTO) for the back contact and aluminum-doped
zinc oxide (AZO)[16] for the front contact[17] enabling connection
to an external circuit. The absorber material where photogener-
ated electron-hole pairs are created was intrinsic hydrogenated
amorphous silicon (a-Si:H). This study focuses on analyzing
the impact of absorber thickness (varied from 22 to 233 nm)
on the performance of the TPV device while keeping other
layers constant.[12] The absorber thickness is critical for optimiza-
tion, as increasing the thickness leads to higher photocurrent
generation,[18] that is, a major number of electron-hole pairs
photogenerated per second,[17] which is reﬂected in an increase
in the short-circuit current density (Jsc). However, as one could
expect it is also observed that a higher thickness results in lower
average photopic transmittance (APT) and color rendering
index (CRI).[19]
It is relevant to highlight that these devices are made to avoid
the use of the cataloged Critical Raw Material (CRM) or toxic/
hazardous materials. In this sense, diborane (which is usually
used for the HTL deposition on traditional amorphous silicon
devices) has been avoided. It is worth mentioning that all the layers
are deposited at relatively low temperatures (below 200 °C) result-
ing in a low thermal-budget fabrication process. Additionally, the
different deposition techniques involved in the device manufactur-
ing allow a conformal and controlled deposition of the different
nanometric layers that compose the solar cell structure.
2. Experimental Design, Results, and Discussion
Planar ultrathin TPV devices were fabricated with the follow-
ing architecture: SLG/FTO/AZO/a-SiCx:H(n)/a-Si:H/V2Ox/AZO.
This work focuses on studying the effect of varying the thickness
of the absorber layers, while AZO, a-SiCx:H(n) and V2Ox are kept
unchanged for a more accurate comparison. For this study, seven
samples were prepared with the following absorber layer thick-
ness: 22, 35, 56, 70, 76, 123, and 233 nm. The absorber deposi-
tion was carried out using a mixture of 36 sccm of silane (SiH4)
and 12 sccm of methane (CH4). Throughout the process, pres-
sure, temperature, and gas ﬂow conditions were kept constant,
with only the deposition time varied to adjust the absorber thick-
ness, as shown in Figure 1.
Once each sample was fully grown, the active area of the cells
was deﬁned and isolated using a conventional UV photolitho-
graphic process (Figure 2a), followed by wet chemical etchings.
In this way, an effective electrical isolation of the cells is achieved
and setting, at the same time, the active cell area (0.25 cm2), as
shown in Figure 2b.
3. Optical Characterization
Transmittance and reﬂectance spectra were employed to deter-
mine the values of APT and CRI, as per the equations provided
in the methodology outlined by Traverse et al.[20] APT was calcu-
lated using Equation (1), where T is the transmission, P is the
photopic response of the human eye, and S is the solar photon
ﬂux (AM1.5G), In this equation, the integration limits were
deﬁned between 380 and 825 nm. For more detailed information
on APT and CRI calculations, see ref. [20] (please note that
ref. [20] names this parameter as average visible transmittance.
However, we establish the nomenclature to be average photopic
transmittance (APT) as it is more precise and also because the
term average visible transmittance can be confounded with
the concept of mean visible transmittance, which does not
account for the human eye’s photopic response P(λ) which gov-
erns our perception of color).

3.2. Optoelectronic Characterization
3.2.1. J–V Characteristics: Power Conversion Efﬁciency and Light
Utilization Efﬁciency
The analysis of these solar cells shows that increasing absorber
thickness enhances current generation and overall efﬁciency
(PCE) but reduces transparency (APT) and color neutrality
(CRI). J–V measurements were made under standard test condi-
tions using a AAA-class solar simulator (1 kW m2 AM1.5G solar
spectrum and 25 °C). Table 2 summarizes the main photovoltaic
parameters, including APT, CRI, and LUE (light utilization efﬁ-
ciency). This last parameter has been proposed as a suitable ﬁg-
ure of merit for TPV devices[20] and is given by the product of the
PCE by the APT. Additionally, the statistics for all the optoelec-
tronic parameters for each sample are presented in Figure S1,
Supporting Information.
Figure 6 shows that increasing the absorber thickness in TPV
devices improves Jsc (almost linear increase with the absorber
thickness as shown in Figure 7b) and, consequently the PCE also
increases. On the other hand, the LUE shows a more complex
behavior since it balances transparency with photovoltaic
performance. The LUE initially increases with the absorber thick-
ness, showing a maximum value in the range of LUE ≈1.3% for
thicknesses in the range of 56–70 nm, and decreases for higher
thicknesses. On the other hand, it is interesting to remark on the
relatively small changes of the LUE in the range of thicknesses
between 35 and 123 nm (S1–S5), with LUE values typically
between 1.21 and 1.33%. This indicates an optimal absorber
thickness range between 35 and 123 nm where PCE and trans-
parency are well balanced. Beyond this range, further increases
in thickness enhance PCE but drastically reduce transparency,
causing a higher decrease in the LUE. In addition, we also
observe a decrease in the ﬁll factor (FF) for the thicker absorbers,
which is likely related to increased internal resistance and recom-
bination losses.
On the other hand, it is also interesting to remark on the rele-
vant values of Voc that are achieved through the whole device
series, with values in the range 785–815 mV (with a record value
of 817 mV for the thicker absorber layer). These values are close
to the record Voc around 900 mV that has been achieved in stan-
dard (opaque) a-Si:H solar cells.

Spectral response measurements are valuable to characterize the
photocurrent and are commonly used to determine the losses
responsible for reducing the measured Jsc from the maximum
achievable photocurrent. EQE is a dimensionless parameter
given by the number of electrons which exit the device per inci-
dent photon at each wavelength. The photocurrent is the integral
over wavelength of the product of the measured EQE with the
illumination spectrum, AM1.5G for terrestrial standard solar
cells.[30] The IQE for transparent solar devices was calculated

IQE ¼ EQE 1 /C0 R /C0 T (7)
As the absorber thickness increases, EQE initially improves

450 nm peak, further reduce efﬁciency. Beyond 600 nm,

material to convert lower energy photons into electron ﬂow

while internal losses can be well managed, further optimization

values. In any case, we can estimate that by reducing reﬂection

4. Conclusion
In this work, the limits of device efﬁciency, transparency, and
LUE have been studied in TPV devices based on the integration
of a nano a-Si:H layer between optimized selective contacts. The
study performed corroborates that the thickness of the absorber
layer is crucial to the overall performance of TPV)devices. As
absorber thickness increases, transparency and color accuracy
decrease. This tradeoff is essential for applications like BIPV,
where both energy efﬁciency and esthetic considerations are
important. Thicker absorbers improve energy conversion at
the expense of transparency and potential color distortion.
There is an optimal thickness range, between 50 and 150 nm,
where a suitable balance between PCE and transparency is
achieved, yielding maximum LUE values in the range of
LUE ≈1.25–1.33%, corresponding to devices with PCE values
up to 2.9% and transparency (APT) in the range of 40–60%.
These constitute world-record LUE values for inorganic TPV
devices. On the other hand, devices are characterized by good
Voc values (in the range of 788–817 mV) and collection efﬁcien-
cies (in the range of 80–90%) for the whole device series, which
can be related to the optimized selective contacts implemented in
these devices. The highest carrier collection efﬁciencies of 90%
are achieved within the thinner absorbers (thickness ≈22 nm)
and this partially compensates for potential efﬁciency losses
related to the deterioration of μτeff observed at these very low
absorber thicknesses, likely related to the inﬂuence of charged
defects at the interfaces.
Finally, reﬂection and EQE/IQE measurements indicate the
presence of reﬂection losses mainly located in the 450 nm spec-
tral range, with the 220 nm AZO layer notably contributing to
these losses. Correction of these losses by suitable adjustment
of TCO thickness and/or implementation of suitable antireﬂec-
tive coatings could allow for a relevant increase of LUE beyond
values in the range of 1.6%.

(ReRa solutions) using an IEEE 488 GPIB Instrument Control Device
(National Instruments GPIB-USB-HS). Spectral response measurements
were acquired using a spectral response system (Bentham PVE300) cali-
brated with Si and Ge photodiodes. For optoelectronic measurements, the
samples have been placed in a dark opaque mat to avoid any back reﬂec-
tions that could alter the characterization of the transparent solar cells.
